components.text: Explain the long history and severe scale of suffering among nonmoral animals under perfectly good theism.
Answer the comparative claim that this suffering is more probable under indifferent naturalism.
Explain why prolonged suffering among nonmoral animals is expected or morally justified under perfectly good theism.
Address the comparative claim that indifferent naturalism predicts this historical pattern more readily.
Address the special evidential force of suffering predating human moral agency.
Explain why a value-oriented creator would produce a universe whose physical volume is overwhelmingly hostile to embodied moral life.
Answer the comparative expectation that near-total hostility is less surprising under naturalism.
Answer why a value-oriented creator would produce a universe almost wholly hostile to embodied moral agents.
Address whether the observed hostile proportion is more expected on naturalism than on theism.
Defend the independent value of cosmic emptiness, scale, or artistry under theism.
Explain sincere nonresistant nonbelief despite a perfectly loving God's alleged desire for relationship with every person.
Explain the uneven cultural and geographic distribution of nonbelief under perfect divine love.
Explain how perfect love can permit sincere nonresistant nonbelief despite the good of relationship with God.
Explain the geographically and historically uneven distribution of religious belief.
Supply a reason applying even when a person is open to belief and relationship.
Answer the claim that objective moral authority and obligation require a personal divine ground.
Answer the separate claim that identifying evil also presupposes natural teleology.
Defeat the claim that objective moral authority and obligation require a divine personal ground.
Provide a nontheistic location for objective normative truth and authority.
Address the separate natural-teleology premise used in the argument from evil.
Answer the claim that irreducible consciousness requires an immaterial soul excluded by naturalism.
Answer the claim that meaningful freedom and responsibility require libertarian alternatives and a soul.
Defeat the inference that consciousness and meaningful freedom require an immaterial soul.
Supply a naturalistic account compatible with irreducible phenomenal consciousness.
Supply a reasons-responsive account of freedom compatible with determinism.
Address the claimed loss of moral responsibility and intellectual integrity.
Answer the inference that causally determined belief cannot be rationally acquired or intellectually responsible.
Answer the distinct evolutionary claim that adaptive selection undercuts the truth reliability of cognition.
Answer the claim that a causally determined belief cannot be rationally acquired or intellectually responsible.
Explain how determination can preserve sensitivity to reasons rather than merely produce behavior.
Answer the claim that evolution selects only adaptive behavior and therefore undercuts confidence in the truth of beliefs.
Explain how belief content becomes causally connected to behavior and environmental success under naturalism.
Defeat the inference from selection for adaptive behavior to a global undercutting defeater for belief reliability.
Explain how belief content can causally influence adaptive behavior.
Explain why successful adaptation generally favors reliable belief-forming mechanisms.
Answer the charge that positing fundamental phenomenal properties is an unsupported or ad hoc naturalistic rescue.
Provide a complete naturalistic explanation of finite unified consciousness without a soul.
Defeat the charge that positing fundamental phenomenal properties is an unmotivated or ad hoc naturalistic rescue.
Explain the evidential motivation supplied by consciousness's apparent reality and irreducibility.
Explain why physical science leaves room for intrinsic phenomenal natures.
Answer the claim that grounding morality in God supplies objectivity unavailable to atheism.
Show that person-grounded moral value is arbitrary or contingent rather than necessarily objective.
Answer whether grounding morality in God's personal nature secures objectivity rather than a subject-dependent standard.
Explain why being grounded in a person entails metaethical subjectivism in the relevant sense.
Explain why necessary, objective moral properties require a personal transcendent ground rather than irreducible normative facts.
Answer the objection that grounding morality in the nature of a person remains metaethical subjectivism.
Answer the circularity concern about why agents are obligated to obey divine commands.
Answer the objection that grounding value in God's nature is merely person-based metaethical subjectivism.
Explain why personal moral properties require a personal rather than abstract ground.
Distinguish a necessary eternal divine person from finite persons and contingent preferences.
Answer the proposed relational or developmental good of cooperative inquiry as a justification for uncertainty about God's existence.
Answer the separate culpability, apostasy, and delayed-conversion reasons offered for hiddenness.
Defeat the claim that nonbelief is needed to preserve cooperative inquiry into God and divine reality.
Show that shared exploration can remain valuable after God's existence is already believed.
Address protective hiddenness based on culpability or anticipated apostasy.
Compare an ultimate divine consciousness with fundamental phenomenal properties as explanations of finite consciousness.
Answer the naturalistic claim that fundamental phenomenal properties can accommodate consciousness without souls.
Answer whether fundamental phenomenal properties adequately explain and predict finite consciousness under naturalism.
Provide a comparative theistic explanation for irreducible finite consciousness.
Address the evidential motivation for treating phenomenal character as fundamental.
Show why appealing to the fall explains the chronology and specific predatory organization of animal suffering.
Show that a fall-based account coheres with evidence of animal predation and suffering before human agents.
Show that bare theism predicts a fall and the observed structure of predation rather than merely permitting them.
Defeat the fall's adequacy as an explanation of prehistoric animal suffering and organized predation.
Test whether a fall account coheres with modern evidence about animal suffering before humans.
Test whether bare theism predicts a fall and its specific predatory consequences.
Address free-will, soul-building, restoration, and compensation alternatives independently of the fall.
